customers.title: Selling 1 — Customers & Selling Foundations
customers.desc: Customers and selling foundations in ZhiftERP: the Customer doctype walk — type, group, territory, the price list and terms resolution chains, the credit section, tax and compliance fields, retirement by the Disabled flag; the Customer Group and Territory tree designs with the behavioural-difference test and the change discipline; contacts and addresses including the multi-site pattern decided by the paying-entity question; payment terms templates, the credit ladder, the limit machinery with the block posture and bypass controls, statements, and the credit review; the onboarding gate with the duplicate check and first-document verification; and the six customer data reads on their cadences.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Customer record: scope and structure
lessons.html:
This module covers the Customer master and the selling foundations in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: create Customer records with the full field set; design the Customer Group and Territory trees; maintain contacts and addresses including multi-site customers; operate credit limits and payment terms under the owner's ladder; run the customer onboarding gate; and run the customer data reads on their cadences.

Where the Customer record sits. Every selling document — Quotation, Sales Order, Delivery Note, Sales Invoice — names a customer, and pulls its behaviour from that customer's record: the price list, the payment terms, the credit limit, the tax treatment, the addresses. A selling document created against a well-built Customer record pre-fills correctly; one created against a thin or wrong record requires per-document correction, and per-document correction is where pricing and terms errors enter.

What reads the Customer record.

1. The selling documents — every transaction in modules 3-7 begins by selecting the customer.
2. The receivables ledger — the Accounts track's customer balances, statements, and aging all key on the record.
3. The pricing machinery — module 2's price lists and pricing rules resolve through the customer's group and record.
4. The credit controls — Chapter 5's limit checks run per customer per company.
5. The reports — sales by territory, receivables by group, customer-wise profitability.

Custody. The sales function operates the records; the owner decides credit limits and payment terms per the ladder (Chapter 5); the accountant owns the receivables side and the tax fields' correctness; record creation runs through the onboarding gate (Chapter 6), by the roles the matrix permits.

Build order. The trees before the records, the records before the documents:

1. The Customer Group tree designed (Chapter 3) — the commercial classification.
2. The Territory tree designed (Chapter 3) — the geography.
3. The onboarding gate written (Chapter 6) — the checklist and the roles.
4. Customers created through the gate, with contacts and addresses (Chapters 2, 4).
5. Credit and terms set per the ladder (Chapter 5).

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Customer doctype walk. Chapter 3: the group and territory trees. Chapter 4: contacts and addresses. Chapter 5: credit and terms. Chapter 6: the onboarding gate. Chapter 7: the customer data reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Customer doctype
lessons.html:
Open Customer (awesome bar) > New. Complete the fields in order.

1. Customer Name. The legal or trading name per the naming convention: the registered name for companies, consistently formatted, without abbreviations that collide. The name prints on every document and statement; it is entered once, correctly, at the gate.

2. Customer Type. Company or Individual — the classification that drives which tax and compliance fields apply, and how the record reads in reporting.

3. Customer Group. The commercial classification from Chapter 3's tree — retail counters, chains, institutions, distributors. The group is a working field, not a label: default price lists and payment terms can derive from it, and the receivables and sales reports aggregate by it. A customer in the wrong group prices from the wrong list.

4. Territory. The geography from Chapter 3's tree. Sales reporting, targets, and territory-based analyses key on it.

5. Currency and Default Price List. The billing currency, and the price list the customer's documents pre-fill from (module 2 covers the lists). The resolution order at document time: the customer's own default, else the group's, else the selling default — the same decided-chain pattern as the stock defaults, and the same rule: the chain is wired once, by convention, and verified.

6. Payment Terms Template. The default terms the customer's invoices carry (Chapter 5). Set from the ladder's decision, not typed ad hoc per invoice.

7. The credit limit section. Per company: the credit limit amount, and the check behaviour (Chapter 5's machinery). The limit is entered here but decided at the ladder; the field carries the decision, and Chapter 7's changes read audits that it moved only by decision.

8. Tax fields. The tax category where the site uses category-based tax rules, and the tax identification numbers per the compliance requirements — for Nigerian B2B customers, the TIN the e-invoicing and statutory reporting require. The accountant rules which fields are mandatory per customer type; the gate enforces them at creation, because a missing TIN prevents the invoice from being submitted when invoicing is due.

9. Disabled. Customers are retired by the Disabled flag at zero balance, never deleted — document history references every customer that ever traded, per the standing retirement pattern.

Verification per record. The name per convention; type correct; group and territory from the trees; price list and terms per the decisions; credit per the ladder; tax fields complete for the type; primary contact and address attached (Chapter 4).

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The Customer Group and Territory trees
lessons.html:
Two trees classify every customer. This chapter is their design procedure.

1. What each tree answers.

1. Customer Group — the commercial question: what kind of buyer is this, and what pricing and terms behaviour follows? Groups drive price list and terms defaults, and the receivables and margin reports aggregate by them.
2. Territory — the geographic question: where is this customer, and which sales responsibility covers them? Territories drive sales reporting and targets.

The two are independent classifications: a chain customer in Ibadan and a retail counter in Ibadan share a territory and differ in group. Designing one tree to answer both questions produces a tree that answers neither cleanly.

2. The Customer Group tree design. Open Customer Group Tree (awesome bar). The design procedure, on paper first per the standing pattern:

1. List the commercial classes the business actually treats differently — different price lists, different terms, different credit postures. For a pharmaceutical distributor: retail counters, chain pharmacies, hospitals and institutions, sub-distributors. A class with no behavioural difference is not a group; it is a report filter at most.
2. Three levels or fewer, per the standing tree rule: the root, the major classes, and subdivisions only where behaviour genuinely differs.
3. Wire the defaults — where a group's members share a price list or terms template, set it at the group so new members inherit; record the wiring in the convention.

3. The Territory tree design. The same procedure for geography: the root, the regions the business manages against (Lagos, South-West, per the sales structure), and cities or zones only where reporting or responsibility requires them. The tree mirrors how sales responsibility is actually assigned — a territory no one owns is a reporting row without a use.

4. The tree change discipline. Both trees change by decision, not per customer: a new group or territory is a structural decision recorded with its reason (what behaviour or responsibility it captures), because each new node fragments the history of the reports that aggregate on it. Reclassifying an existing customer is an ordinary edit with a note; restructuring a tree mid-year is a governed event with the report consumers told.

5. The classification read. Quarterly: customers per group and territory, sampled against the definitions — the retail counter that grew into a chain and was never regrouped prices from the wrong list until this read finds it. The read closes with the corrections applied and the fragmenting-node check: groups or territories with a handful of members and no behavioural difference are merge candidates for the next structural review.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Contacts and addresses
lessons.html:
Contacts and addresses are separate records linked to the customer. This chapter is their structure and the multi-site pattern.

1. The Contact record. One record per person: name, designation, phone, email, linked to the customer (a contact can link to several parties). Per customer:

1. The primary contact — the default the documents and communications pull.
2. Role-specific contacts — the buyer, the accounts payable contact for statements and collections (Chapter 5's statements go to a named person, not a company), the receiving contact per site where deliveries need one.

2. The Address record. One record per physical address: lines, city, state, country, linked to the customer, with two flags:

1. Preferred Billing Address — where invoices and statements address.
2. Preferred Shipping Address — where deliveries default.

Documents pull the preferred addresses and allow per-document override — the delivery to a different site selects that site's address on the document, and the address prints on the delivery paperwork the driver carries.

3. The multi-site customer pattern. A chain with many branches and one payer is one Customer record — the payer — with one billing address and many shipping addresses (one per branch, named by the branch: the chain's own branch codes in the address title keep the picker unambiguous). The consequences, stated:

1. One receivables balance — the chain owes as one account; statements, credit limit, and collections run against the payer, which is how the chain itself operates.
2. Per-branch delivery — each Delivery Note selects its branch's shipping address; the delivery history per branch remains readable by address.
3. The alternative — child customers per branch — is used only where branches genuinely pay separately, because separate Customer records mean separate balances, separate credit limits, and statements the chain's head office did not ask for. The pattern is decided at onboarding from one question: who pays?

4. Address and contact hygiene. The details that age fastest in any register are people and addresses. The standing read, quarterly: primary contacts confirmed current for the top accounts (the collections function surfaces dead contacts naturally — a statement that bounces is a hygiene finding); shipping addresses sampled against recent delivery paperwork; leaver contacts at customer organisations replaced when known. Hygiene findings are ordinary edits with dates — the record's history shows when the business knew.

5. What does not go in contacts and addresses. Terms, prices, and credit notes belong on the customer and its documents, not in contact remarks; delivery instructions that are permanent belong on the address record; per-order instructions belong on the order. The rule keeps each fact where the documents that need it will read it.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Credit and terms
lessons.html:
Credit is the business lending money to its customers. This chapter is the machinery and the controls.

1. Payment Terms Templates. Open Payment Terms Template (awesome bar) > New: named templates — Cash, 30 Days, 45 Days, or split terms (a percentage on invoice, the balance at a due interval). Templates are the only lawful source of terms: the ladder decides which template a customer receives; the template sets due dates on every invoice automatically; and the receivables aging (the Accounts track) computes from those due dates. Terms typed per invoice bypass the decision and corrupt the aging.

2. The terms and credit ladder. The written policy, owner-approved, that decides who may extend what:

1. Cash terms — the default for new customers below the threshold; no approval needed.
2. Credit terms within standard bands (30 or 45 days, limits per band) — approved by the sales manager per the ladder's figures, with the customer's trade references or history documented.
3. Above-band terms or limits — the owner's decision, documented.

Every credit decision files with the customer: the approved band, the approver, the date, the basis. Credit extended without its documented decision is Chapter 9's first error.

3. The credit limit machinery. On the Customer record, per company: the limit amount and the enforcement behaviour. At document submission the system checks outstanding balance plus the new document against the limit:

1. The block — the standard posture: a Sales Order or Invoice that would exceed the limit does not submit.
2. The bypass role — the named role (per the matrix) that may submit over the limit; every bypass is a decision by that role, visible in the document trail, and the monthly over-limit read lists each one with its approver.
3. Ignore-check settings exist per customer for the rare standing exception — a register row with the owner's reason, not a convenience toggle.

4. Statements and the collections tie. The Statement of Accounts per customer — the invoice, payment, and balance history — sends on the monthly cadence to the accounts payable contact (Chapter 4), and on demand at collection conversations. Statements are the customer's view of Chapter 5 working: terms on every invoice, due dates computed, payments allocated. The collections procedures themselves belong to module 7; this chapter's contribution is the data they run on.

5. The credit review. Per the calendar: top exposures reviewed quarterly (limit against payment behaviour — the aging per customer from the Accounts track's reports); limits raised or reduced by the ladder with the decision filed; the annual full pass over all credit customers riding the receivables year-end. Credit that is never reviewed only moves in one direction — upward, one exception at a time — which is what the review exists to prevent.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The onboarding gate
lessons.html:
Customers enter the register by gate. This chapter is the checklist and its operation.

1. Why a gate. Every field Chapter 2 walked is quick to complete at creation and costly to correct after documents exist: the wrong group prices documents until the classification read finds it; the missing TIN blocks invoicing at month-end; the undecided terms become whatever the first invoice typed. The gate is fifteen minutes that ends those cases.

2. The gate checklist. In order:

1. The duplicate check first — the register searched by name fragments, phone, email, and TIN before creation. A duplicate customer splits one buyer's history and balance across records: credit checked against half the exposure, statements that disagree with the customer's own ledger, and a merge remediation later. One minute at the gate.
2. The paying-entity question — who pays? The answer decides the Chapter 4 pattern: one record with many shipping addresses, or separate customers. Asked and recorded at the gate, because restructuring after documents exist is a remediation.
3. Classification — group and territory from the trees, per the definitions.
4. Terms and credit per the ladder — cash by default; credit only with its documented decision (Chapter 5).
5. Tax and compliance fields — TIN and the mandatory fields per customer type, verified against the customer's documents, because compliance fields transcribed from a phone call are the invoicing blocks of the following month.
6. Contacts and addresses — the primary pair at minimum; the accounts payable contact for credit customers; the shipping set for multi-site customers.
7. The first-document check — a draft quotation against the new record, confirming the price list, terms, and addresses pre-fill as intended; the draft deleted.

3. Who operates the gate. Customer creation is permitted to the roles the matrix names — the sales function's designated users — with the credit fields writable per the ladder's roles only. Bulk imports (a customer book migration) run as governed imports against the same checklist columns, sampled after load per the import procedure.

4. The gate's monthly read. Customers created in the month sampled against the checklist: fields complete, decisions filed, duplicates absent. A gate that is not read drifts into a form-filling exercise; the monthly sample is what keeps the fifteen minutes honest, and its findings feed the checklist's next revision.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The customer data reads
lessons.html:
The standing reads that keep the customer register true, each with its cadence and action.

1. The duplicate-candidate read — monthly. Near-identical names, shared phones or TINs across records, flagged for review. Confirmed duplicates merge per the remediation procedure (documents re-pointed per the data-fix rules, one surviving record); near-misses are noted so the next gate search finds them. The read requires little effort while the register is small, and becomes essential once collections depend on complete balances.

2. The classification read — quarterly (Chapter 3). Group and territory sampled against the definitions; regrades applied; fragmenting nodes flagged for the structural review.

3. The credit changes read — monthly. Every change to a credit limit or terms template in the month, with who changed it, listed against the ladder's filed decisions. The read is the audit that the fields move only by decision: a limit that moved without its paper is corrected and the permission gap closed. The over-limit bypass list (Chapter 5) files alongside it — the two together are the credit control's monthly evidence.

4. The dormancy read — quarterly. Customers with no documents across the window, split by class: credit customers with open balances and no activity route to collections (module 7); cash customers with no activity for the policy's period are candidates for the disabled flag at the annual pass. Dormant records with live credit limits are the specific finding — an unused limit is exposure with no relationship watching it, and the read reduces it by decision.

5. The hygiene read — quarterly (Chapter 4). Contacts and addresses for the top accounts confirmed current; bounce findings from statements actioned.

6. The receivables tie. The customer register's ultimate read belongs to the Accounts track: the receivables aging per customer, monthly, with the statements cycle. This module's registers exist so that read is trustworthy — one record per payer, terms from templates, limits by decision. Where the aging surfaces a register problem (a balance split across duplicates, terms that disagree with the filed decision), the finding routes back to this module's remediation lanes, and the correction is made in the register, not worked around in the report.

7. The reads' filing. Each read's output — the list, the corrections, the date — files with the sales function's records per the one-lookup standard, and the quarterly reads ride the same calendar as the stock and access recertifications so the review rhythm is one habit, not five.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: HealthTrade onboards the chain
lessons.html:
This chapter applies Chapters 2-7 to a real onboarding: a chain pharmacy group approaching HealthTrade for supply. Configuration values and outcomes are listed per step.

The prospect. A chain pharmacy group with 30 branches — 24 in Lagos, 6 in Ibadan — requests a supply relationship: central purchasing, head-office payment, deliveries to branches.

Step 1 — the paying-entity question (Chapters 4, 6). Asked first at the gate: who pays? The answer — head office pays for all branches — decides the pattern: one Customer record (the group's registered company), one receivables balance, one credit limit, with per-branch shipping addresses. The alternative (30 child customers) is recorded as considered and rejected with the reason: the chain pays as one entity, and 30 balances would manufacture reconciliation work both sides.

Step 2 — the record built (Chapter 2). Customer Type: Company; Customer Group: Chain Pharmacies (the group whose defaults carry the trade price list); Territory: the group's head-office territory, with sales reporting noting the two-city footprint. Tax fields: the TIN verified against the chain's registration documents at the gate. The duplicate check runs first and returns clean.

Step 3 — addresses and contacts (Chapter 4). One billing address (head office); 30 shipping addresses, titled with the chain's own branch codes so document pickers are unambiguous. Contacts: the head-office buyer (primary), the accounts payable contact (statements), and the two regional operations contacts for delivery coordination.

Step 4 — terms and credit (Chapter 5). The chain requests credit terms. Per the ladder: the requested volume places the decision above the standard bands, so it goes to the owner with the trade references and the opening-volume projection. The decision, filed with the record: 45-day terms on the named template, an opening credit limit per the projection, review scheduled at ninety days. The limit enters the record's credit section with the block posture standard; the bypass role confirmed as the named holders only.

Step 5 — the first-document check and the first cycle (Chapters 6-7). The draft quotation confirms pre-fill: trade price list from the group, 45-day terms from the template, head-office billing, branch shipping selectable. The first month's documents flow: orders from head office, deliveries per branch address, invoices to the payer, the first statement to the named accounts payable contact. The ninety-day credit review runs on schedule against actual payment behaviour, and the limit decision is re-filed with the review's data — the ladder operating as procedure rather than exception.

The register evidence. The gate file holds the duplicate check, the paying-entity decision, the classification, the credit decision and review, and the first-document check — the onboarding answerable from one folder, per the standing standard.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in customer foundations, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — credit without a decision. Symptom: terms typed per invoice; limits set in conversation; the aging computed from improvised due dates. Correction: templates applied, the ladder's decisions filed retroactively where defensible, limits reviewed. Prevention: terms only from templates, credit only from the ladder, and the monthly changes read.

Error 2 — the duplicate customer. Symptom: one buyer's history and balance split across records; credit checked against partial exposure; statements the customer disputes. Correction: the merge remediation with documents re-pointed. Prevention: the gate's duplicate check first, and the monthly candidate read.

Error 3 — the wrong multi-site pattern. Symptom: 30 child customers for one payer, or one record for branches that pay separately; balances that match nobody's ledger. Correction: the restructure remediation per the data-fix rules. Prevention: the paying-entity question asked and recorded at the gate.

Error 4 — classification drift. Symptom: customers priced from the wrong list because their group no longer matches their behaviour; territory reports that mislead. Correction: regrades from the classification read. Prevention: the quarterly read against the definitions and the tree change discipline.

Error 5 — compliance fields at invoicing time. Symptom: missing TINs discovered when the invoice will not submit; month-end blocked on data entry. Correction: the fields completed from the customer's documents. Prevention: the gate's mandatory-fields step, verified against documents at creation.

Error 6 — the unwatched limit. Symptom: dormant customers with live limits; credit that only ever ratchets upward; bypasses nobody lists. Correction: the dormancy and over-limit reads run, limits reduced by decision. Prevention: the quarterly credit review and the monthly bypass list.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the Customer doctype walk including the resolution chains, the credit section, and the retirement rule; design both trees with the behavioural-difference test and the change discipline; structure contacts and addresses including the multi-site pattern from the paying-entity question; operate templates, the ladder, the limit machinery with its bypass controls, statements, and the credit review; run the onboarding gate end to end; and run the six data reads on their cadences.

Module rule 1: every selling document stands on its Customer record — created through the gate with the duplicate check and the paying-entity question, classified by the trees, carrying terms only from templates and credit only from the ladder's filed decisions, and kept true by the scheduled reads. Module 2 covers items and price lists.

items_prices.title: Selling 2 — Items & Price Lists
items_prices.desc: Items and price lists in ZhiftERP selling: the commercial field walk on the one register record — codes, names as customers read them, item groups, Is Sales Item, and the sales defaults; units of measure with verified conversion factors, the Sales UOM, and the unit-column discipline; the class-based price list architecture with the resolution chain and what lists are not; Item Price maintenance through the governed update with the changes and completeness reads; Pricing Rules — scope, condition, effect, priority, and the register — for quantity breaks and promotions; and item tax classification by the accountant's ruling with the quarterly read.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The item's selling side: scope and structure
lessons.html:
This module covers items and price lists from the selling side in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: complete the item's commercial field set; configure units of measure and sales units with their conversions; design the price list architecture; maintain Item Price records by governed update; build Pricing Rules for quantity breaks and structured discounts; verify the item-side tax fields; and run the pricing reads.

One record, several owners. The Item is one record read by several functions, and each function owns its section: the Inventory track owns the stock flags, defaults, and identity settings (Inventory modules 1 and 3); the Accounts track owns the account derivations and tax correctness; this module owns the commercial section — how the item names, sells, converts, and prices. The one-record principle means the selling side never creates a second record for a product that exists; it completes the commercial section of the record the register already holds, through the item creation gate the Inventory track defined, so one product always has one history across stock and sales.

What selling reads from the Item.

1. The identity fields — code, name, description, image: what prints on quotations, orders, and invoices.
2. The item group — the classification driving sales reporting, tax and account derivations, and pricing rule scopes.
3. The units — the stock unit and the sales units with conversion factors (Chapter 3): what quantity means on a document.
4. The prices — through the price lists and Item Price records (Chapters 4-5), and the Pricing Rules layered above them (Chapter 6).
5. The tax classification — the item-side field the tax machinery reads (Chapter 7; module 6 covers the machinery).

Custody. The sales function maintains the commercial section; price changes move only by the governed update procedure (Chapter 5); pricing rules are register entries with owners and reasons (Chapter 6); and the module's standing rule follows the programme's pattern: a price is a decision with a record, never a figure typed at document time.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the commercial field walk. Chapter 3: units of measure and sales units. Chapter 4: the price list architecture. Chapter 5: Item Price maintenance. Chapter 6: Pricing Rules. Chapter 7: item tax fields. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The commercial field walk
lessons.html:
Open the Item record (created through the Inventory track's gate). Complete the commercial fields in order.

1. Item Code. Per the written coding convention — short, unique, structured (PARA-500 for Paracetamol 500mg). The code is the register's handle: it prints on documents, keys every report, and is typed and scanned daily. Codes are permanent; a product whose code must change is retired and re-created through the lifecycle procedures, because documents reference codes forever.

2. Item Name and Description. The name as customers should read it on documents — Paracetamol 500mg Tablets — complete, consistently formatted, without internal abbreviations customers will not recognise. The description field carries the longer print text where documents need it. Both print exactly as entered; the verification is reading a draft document, not the form.

3. Item Group. The classification from the item group tree — analgesics, antibiotics, consumables, per the register's design. The group is a working field on the selling side: sales reports aggregate by it, tax and account derivations can key on it, and Pricing Rules scope by it (Chapter 6). The tree follows the standing design rules: classes the business treats differently, three levels or fewer, changes by decision.

4. The unit fields. The Stock UOM (the unit balances count in — the Inventory track's decision) and the sales-side unit configuration Chapter 3 covers. The commercial walk confirms them; it does not change them casually, because unit changes are posting-behaviour changes under the lifecycle's change governance.

5. Is Sales Item. The flag that admits the item to selling documents. Items the business stocks but does not sell (consumables, spares) leave it off; the flag is the clean answer to why an item does not appear in a document picker.

6. The sales defaults. Per company where used: the default income account and cost center derivations the Accounts track governs — confirmed present per the accountant's design, because a missing derivation surfaces as an accounting question on the first invoice.

7. Image. Where the business prints or displays catalogues and the POS uses images, the image field per the site's convention.

Verification per item. The code per convention; the name as a customer should read it; the group per the tree; the units confirmed; Is Sales Item correct; the defaults present; then one draft quotation row — the code, name, unit, and price appearing as intended — deleted after reading.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Units of measure and sales units
lessons.html:
Customers buy in different units of the same product. This chapter is the unit machinery.

1. The UOM records. Open UOM (awesome bar): the unit master — Unit, Carton-12, Box, Pack. Units are shared records created once per the register's naming; a new unit is a register decision, not a per-item improvisation, because Carton-12 and Ctn-12 as separate records split conversion history.

2. The item's conversion table. On the Item, the UOM conversion table: one row per alternative unit with its factor — Carton-12 = 12 units where the stock unit is the single unit. The rules:

1. The factor states how many stock units one alternative unit contains. Every document row entered in an alternative unit converts to stock units by this factor for all stock and value arithmetic.
2. Factors come from the physical product, verified at the register (the supplier's carton contents counted, not assumed) — a wrong factor mis-converts every document that uses the unit, and the Inventory track's UoM error family (the carton-rate-against-unit-line receipt, the fractional batch balances) is this table wrong or misread.
3. Factor changes are governed events: a supplier changing carton contents is a dated change with the affected prices reviewed (Chapter 5), because the price per carton and the factor move together or the per-unit price silently changes.

3. The Sales UOM. The item's default selling unit — the unit document rows pre-fill with. Set it to how the majority channel buys; rows can select any converted unit per transaction. The standing retail-and-trade pattern: retail counters buy by the unit; chains and institutions buy by the carton — one item record serving both through the conversion table, with the price architecture (Chapters 4-6) carrying the price per unit and per carton per list.

4. Units on documents. The document row carries the quantity, the unit, and the conversion — and prints the unit the customer ordered in. The operator's rules:

1. The unit column is read, not assumed: 50 on a row means 50 of the row's unit; the order for 50 cartons entered as 50 units under-ships by the factor, and the checking discipline on orders and deliveries (modules 4-5) names the unit column explicitly for this reason.
2. Prices follow the unit (Chapter 5's per-UoM prices where used): the rate on the row is per the row's unit, and the row amount is quantity times rate in that unit — readable arithmetic on every row.

5. The conversion read. Quarterly, riding the item lifecycle reads: conversion factors sampled against physical products for the top-selling items; new units created in the quarter checked against the register; items selling in units their table does not carry (a workaround pattern) corrected by adding the decided unit rather than by per-document arithmetic.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The price list architecture
lessons.html:
Prices live on lists; customers resolve to a list. This chapter is the architecture.

1. The Price List record. Open Price List (awesome bar) > New: the name, the currency, and the Selling flag (buying lists belong to the Procurement track). A price list is a named pricing context — a set of Item Prices (Chapter 5) that applies to the customers who resolve to it.

2. The standing architecture. Design the list set from the commercial classes module 1's Customer Group tree defined — the lists and the groups are the same design read from two sides:

1. Standard Selling (retail) — the counter and default prices.
2. Trade — the chain, institution, and distributor prices.
3. Additional lists only where a class genuinely prices differently as a class — a list per customer is an anti-pattern (customer-specific arrangements are Pricing Rules or negotiated document prices with their approvals, not private lists), because every list is a full price set to maintain, and the maintenance cost of Chapter 5 multiplies by the list count.

3. The resolution, restated. Module 1 wired it: the document's price list resolves from the customer's default, else the customer group's, else the selling default. The consequence for this module: putting a customer in the right group is a pricing act. The classification read (module 1, Chapter 3) is therefore also a pricing control, and the wrong-group customer is the wrong-list customer.

4. Currency rules. Each list carries one currency; a customer billing in another currency needs a list in that currency or the exchange-rate machinery the Accounts track governs applied at document time per the site's configuration. For the standing Nigeria-first case: naira lists, with foreign-currency arrangements as the documented exception they are.

5. What price lists are not.

1. Not discounts: a percentage relationship between lists (trade at a margin below retail) is maintained by the update procedure's arithmetic, not by a discount mechanism — the list states the price, and the document shows the price, which keeps document reading simple and disputes short.
2. Not history: superseded prices are history the Item Price records and the update files carry (Chapter 5); the list always states the current price.
3. Not per-document overrides: the negotiated price on one order is that document's rate with its approval per module 4's rules; the list does not move for one order.

6. The architecture read. Annually, with the pricing review: the list set against the customer groups (one behavioural class, one list), orphan lists (no customers resolve to them) retired, and the resolution sampled — five customers per group, a draft document each, the pre-filled list confirmed.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Item Price maintenance
lessons.html:
An Item Price is one item's price on one list. This chapter is the record and the governed update.

1. The Item Price record. Open Item Price (awesome bar): the item, the price list, the rate, and — where the site uses them — the UOM the rate applies to, minimum quantity, and validity dates. The standing shape:

1. One row per item per list for the base case: PARA-500 on Standard Selling at the unit rate; PARA-500 on Trade at the trade rate.
2. Per-UoM rows where the same list prices units and cartons separately — the unit rate and the Carton-12 rate as two rows on the same list, each applying when the document row's unit matches. The carton rate and the conversion factor are maintained together (Chapter 3's rule).
3. Validity dates where prices are scheduled — the dated price change entered in advance, effective automatically.

2. The governed update procedure. Prices change by decision, on a cycle, through one procedure:

1. The decision — the pricing review (the owner's cadence: monthly or per supplier cost events) produces the approved price file: item, list, old rate, new rate, effective date, and the basis (the cost change, the margin decision — module 5 of Inventory supplies the cost side; the margin arithmetic is the accountant's review).
2. The load — the approved file applied by governed import or entry, by the roles the matrix permits, on the effective date or with validity dates.
3. The verification — a sample of updated items drafted on documents per list, rates confirmed; the file and verification filed with the review.

3. Why the procedure is strict. The price fields are among the most financially consequential editable figures in the system: a wrong rate prices every document until noticed, and an unauthorised change is a margin loss attributable to a specific user account. The controls follow: price-write permission held narrowly per the matrix; the monthly price changes read (below) listing every Item Price change against the approved files; and no price typed at document time except as the negotiated, approved document rate module 4 governs.

4. The price changes read — monthly. Every Item Price created or modified in the month, with who and when, reconciled against the approved price files. Changes without a file are corrected and their permission gap closed — the same fields-move-only-by-decision audit as the credit changes read, applied to prices.

5. The completeness read — monthly. Sales items without a current price on their group's list (the picker will fetch nothing, and the document will demand a typed rate — the exact door the module keeps closed); expired validity rows whose successors were never loaded. Both lists worked to zero with the update cycle.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Pricing Rules
lessons.html:
Structured price behaviour — quantity breaks, class discounts, promotions — is configured as Pricing Rules, not typed as document discounts. This chapter is the doctype and its register.

1. The Pricing Rule doctype. Open Pricing Rule (awesome bar) > New. The record in three parts:

1. The scope — what it applies to: item, item group, or brand; and for whom — customer, customer group, or territory. The scope fields make the rule as narrow or broad as the decision: one item for one customer group, or a whole group for all trade customers.
2. The condition — when it applies: minimum (and maximum) quantity or amount thresholds, and validity dates. Quantity thresholds are the quantity-break mechanism: from 50 units, the rate becomes ₦950 is a rule with min qty 50.
3. The effect — what it does: a rate (replacing the list price), a discount percentage, or a discount amount, applied per the rule's price-or-discount configuration.

2. Priority and interaction. Where multiple rules could apply to one row, the priority field and the rule settings decide which wins; the site's standing convention: rules are designed not to overlap, and where an overlap is intended (a promotion superseding a standing break), the priority is set explicitly and recorded. An undesigned overlap prices documents by accident, and the register (below) exists to make every rule's scope visible before a new one is added.

3. Pricing Rules versus the other pricing instruments — the decision table.

1. The price list — the standing price per class: who you are decides the list.
2. The Pricing Rule — structured, conditional behaviour on top of the list: how much or when you buy changes the price, by a written rule with dates.
3. The document-level discount or negotiated rate — the one-off commercial decision on one document, with its approval per module 4's rules.

Each instrument leaves its own evidence, and the separation exists for that reason: the list states the standing position, the rule states the standing condition, and the document shows the exception with its approver.

4. The pricing rules register. One table, per the standing register pattern: each active rule with its scope, condition, effect, owner, reason, and validity — reviewed at the pricing review. Rules without owners or with lapsed reasons are disabled at the review; promotions carry end dates at creation so lapsing is automatic rather than remembered.

5. The rules read — monthly. New and changed rules against the register; expired promotions confirmed inactive; and the effect sample — three documents drafted inside rule conditions (the 50-unit row confirming ₦950) and three outside them (the 49-unit row confirming the list rate), verifying the machinery prices as the register says it should.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Item tax fields
lessons.html:
Tax computation is module 6's subject; this chapter is the item's side of it — the classification the machinery reads.

1. The item tax template field. On the Item (or derived from its item group per the site's design): the Item Tax Template that states the item's tax treatment — standard-rated or exempt, per the tax categories the accountant defines. For a Nigerian pharmaceutical register the distinction is live: many pharmaceutical items are VAT-exempt while general goods are standard-rated, and the item-side field is where each product's treatment is stated once.

2. Why the field lives on the item. The document's tax computation (module 6) combines the document-level tax template with the item-level treatment: a mixed basket — exempt pharmaceuticals and standard-rated consumables on one invoice — taxes correctly per line because each item carries its own classification. The alternative (per-document tax editing) taxes whole documents by operator memory, which is a compliance error generator.

3. Setting the classification.

1. By class, at the gate: the item's tax treatment follows its class per the accountant's ruling table — the item group or the class row states the template, and the gate applies it at creation with the other class-row settings (the Inventory track's control register pattern extended to tax).
2. Changes are governed: a reclassification (a product's exemption status changing by regulation) is a dated decision from the accountant, applied through the change procedure, with the effective date recorded — because tax treatment changes are exactly the changes an auditor asks about.

4. The item tax read — quarterly, with the accountant. The register sampled by class: exempt classes carrying exempt templates, standard classes carrying standard ones, exceptions listed and resolved. New items created in the quarter checked against the ruling table. The read is the selling side's contribution to the tax compliance the Accounts track owns; module 6 adds the document-side reads.

5. The boundary, stated. The selling function applies the accountant's rulings; it does not make them. A customer's request to be invoiced without tax, an item whose treatment seems wrong, a new product class without a ruling — each routes to the accountant as a question, and the document waits for the ruling rather than improvising one. The item tax field carries a decided answer or it carries nothing; there is no operator-judgment lane in tax classification.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: HealthTrade's selling architecture
lessons.html:
This chapter applies Chapters 2-7 to HealthTrade's item and pricing build. Configuration values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the commercial section completed (Chapter 2). The register's items — created through the Inventory gate — receive their commercial walk: codes per the convention (PARA-500), names as customers read them (Paracetamol 500mg Tablets), groups per the tree (Analgesics under Pharmaceuticals), Is Sales Item confirmed, defaults per the accountant's design. The draft-row verification runs per class sample.

Step 2 — the unit set (Chapter 3). The two-channel reality is configured on one record: stock unit Unit; the conversion table carrying Carton-12 = 12 units, the factor verified against the physical carton at the register. Sales UOM set to Unit (the retail majority); trade documents select Carton-12 per row. The rule filed with the register: the carton price and the factor are maintained together.

Step 3 — the lists (Chapter 4). Two selling lists, matching the customer group design from module 1: Standard Selling (retail counters) and Trade (chain pharmacies, institutions, distributors — the module 1 chain resolves here through its group). No per-customer lists; the architecture note records the rejection with the reason.

Step 4 — the prices loaded (Chapter 5). The approved price file loads per list, with per-UoM rows where trade sells cartons: PARA-500 carrying its unit rate on Standard Selling, and its unit and Carton-12 rates on Trade. The verification sample drafts documents per list; the file and sample file with the review.

Step 5 — the quantity break as a rule (Chapter 6). The trade volume decision — from 50 units, the rate becomes ₦950 — is configured as a Pricing Rule: scope PARA-500 for the Trade customer groups, condition min qty 50, effect the rate, validity open, owner and reason in the register. The rules read's effect sample confirms both sides: the 50-unit draft row prices at ₦950; the 49-unit row prices at the list rate.

Step 6 — the tax classifications (Chapter 7). The ruling table applies by class: the exempt pharmaceutical classes carry the exempt template; consumables carry standard-rated. The mixed-basket draft — pharmaceuticals and consumables on one document — taxes per line correctly, and the quarterly read's first pass returns clean.

Step 7 — the first update cycle (Chapter 5). A supplier cost change triggers the month's pricing review: the affected items' new rates approved with the margin arithmetic, loaded on the effective date, verified by sample, filed. The price changes read reconciles the month's Item Price modifications to the approved file exactly — the fields-move-only-by-decision audit passing on its first live month.

The architecture evidence. The register holds: the coding and naming conventions, the unit register with verified factors, the two-list architecture note, the approved price files with verifications, the pricing rules register with the one active rule, and the tax ruling table — the pricing system answerable from one set of documents.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in items and pricing, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the typed price. Symptom: rates entered at document time because the list has no price; margins varying by operator; disputes with no reference. Correction: the completeness read run, missing prices loaded by the update procedure. Prevention: every sales item priced on its group's list, and document-time rates reserved for approved negotiated cases only.

Error 2 — the second item record. Symptom: a selling-side duplicate created for a product the register holds; stock and sales history split. Correction: the merge remediation per the lifecycle rules. Prevention: the one-record principle — the commercial section is completed on the existing record, through the gate.

Error 3 — the wrong conversion factor. Symptom: carton documents mis-converting; fractional balances; the carton price and per-unit price disagreeing silently. Correction: the factor corrected as a governed change with affected prices reviewed. Prevention: factors verified against physical product, and the factor-and-price-together rule.

Error 4 — the list per customer. Symptom: dozens of lists, each a full price set; updates missing lists; maintenance consuming the pricing function. Correction: lists consolidated to the class architecture; customer specifics moved to rules or approved document rates. Prevention: one behavioural class, one list — and the annual architecture read.

Error 5 — the unregistered rule. Symptom: pricing rules accumulating without owners; overlaps pricing documents by accident; expired promotions still firing. Correction: the register rebuilt, orphan rules disabled, priorities set explicitly. Prevention: every rule a register row at creation, end dates on promotions, and the monthly rules read with its effect sample.

Error 6 — tax by operator memory. Symptom: per-document tax editing; mixed baskets taxed wholesale; exemptions applied on request. Correction: item classifications completed per the ruling table; document tax editing withdrawn per the matrix. Prevention: the item-side template by class at the gate, changes only by the accountant's dated ruling, and the quarterly read.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the commercial field walk with the code and naming conventions; operate the UoM table with verified factors and the sales unit; design the class-based list architecture and state what lists are not; maintain Item Prices through the governed update with the changes and completeness reads; build Pricing Rules with scope, condition, effect, and the register; and apply item tax classifications by ruling with the boundary respected.

Module rule 2: a price is a decision with a record — items selling from their one register record, units converting by verified factors, prices living on class lists and moving only by the governed update, conditions expressed as registered Pricing Rules, and tax treatment stated per the accountant's ruling — never a figure typed at document time. Module 3 covers quotations.

quotations.title: Selling 3 — Quotations
quotations.desc: Quotations in ZhiftERP: the field walk — party and list header checks, the row discipline, taxes per template, terms selected not typed, and the pre-issue verification; the rate discipline — pre-fill first, the deviation ladder with specific named concessions, margin visibility, and the monthly deviations read; validity and the revision procedure with the negotiation file; the offer pack — owned terms templates, print discipline, and the transmission record; the pipeline reads — open quotations, outcome marking with reason codes, the conversion read, and deviation-versus-outcome; and conversion to order with the four checks, partial acceptance, and the clean handoff.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Quotation: scope and position
lessons.html:
This module covers the Quotation in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: complete the Quotation field walk; apply the rate discipline including the deviation ladder; operate validity and the revision procedure; assemble the offer pack with terms templates; run the pipeline reads; and convert won quotations to Sales Orders.

What a Quotation is. The Quotation is the business's written offer: these items, these quantities, these prices, these terms, valid until this date. Everything downstream — the Sales Order, the deliveries, the invoices — inherits what the quotation states. The offer is therefore built from the registers (modules 1-2) rather than composed freehand: the customer from the gate, the items from the register, the rates from the lists and rules, the terms from the templates.

Where quotations sit in the flow.

1. Upstream: the request arrives from an existing customer, or from a prospect. Prospect and opportunity handling belongs to the CRM lane where the site runs one; the boundary rule is that a Quotation to a prospect still runs through the customer gate before or at conversion — no order ships to a party the register has not onboarded.
2. Downstream: the accepted quotation converts to the Sales Order (module 4) — the commitment document. The quotation is the offer; the order is the agreement; the distinction carries through every procedure in this module.

When a quotation is required. Per the written policy: counter and routine trade sales transact without quotations (the standing lists price them); quotations are required for enterprise and institutional business, for anything negotiated, for tender responses, and above the value threshold the policy sets. The requirement exists because a negotiated arrangement without a written offer becomes a dispute with no reference document.

Custody. The sales function prepares and issues quotations; rate deviations follow the approval ladder (Chapter 3); revisions follow the versioning procedure (Chapter 4); and the standing rule for the module: an issued offer is a record — it expires by its date, changes by revision, and is never silently edited.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Quotation field walk. Chapter 3: rates and the deviation ladder. Chapter 4: validity and revisions. Chapter 5: terms and the offer pack. Chapter 6: the pipeline reads. Chapter 7: conversion to order. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Quotation doctype
lessons.html:
Open Quotation (awesome bar) > New. Complete the fields in order.

1. Quotation To and Party. Customer (the register record) or Lead where the site quotes prospects. Selecting the customer pulls module 1's machinery: the price list, the currency, the terms default, the addresses and contact. The pre-fill is the intended behaviour — verify it rather than retype it.

2. Date and Valid Till. The issue date, and the expiry date of the offer. Valid Till is a commitment boundary, not a formality: Chapter 4 covers its discipline. It is set per the policy's standard window (and shortened for volatile-cost items), never left blank.

3. Order Type. Sales for the standing case; the other types where the site uses them (maintenance, shopping cart) per their flows.

4. Currency and Price List. Pre-filled from the customer's resolution chain (module 2, Chapter 4). A quotation on the wrong list is wrong on every row; the header check takes two seconds and precedes any row work.

5. The items table. One row per offered line:

1. Item Code — from the register; the description prints as module 2 entered it.
2. Qty and UOM — the quantity in the stated unit, per module 2's unit-column discipline.
3. Rate — pre-filled from the list and any applying Pricing Rules; deviations only per Chapter 3's ladder.
4. Amount — quantity times rate, per row, readable arithmetic.

6. Taxes and Charges. The tax template per the customer and document context; item-level treatments (module 2, Chapter 7) compute per line. The tax total on the offer is the tax total the invoice will show — quoting tax-exclusive and invoicing tax-inclusive causes disputes; the template discipline prevents it.

7. Terms and Conditions. The T&C template per Chapter 5 — selected, not typed.

8. Totals, discounts, and margin. The document-level discount fields exist and are governed by the same ladder as row deviations (Chapter 3). Before submission, the margin view (where the site exposes it per role) is read: an offer is a commercial commitment, and the preparer confirms it clears the floor the policy sets or carries the approval that authorises the exception.

9. Save, review, submit, send. Draft for internal review per the value threshold; submit to issue; send as the offer pack (Chapter 5). Submission fixes the record — from this point the offer changes only by Chapter 4's revision procedure.

Verification per quotation. The party and list correct; validity set; every row's unit and rate read; taxes per template; terms selected; margin cleared or approved; then the print preview read as the customer will read it, because the document the customer receives is the record the business must honour.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Rates and the deviation ladder
lessons.html:
Quotation rates start at the register's prices and deviate only by decision. This chapter is the discipline.

1. The pre-fill is the default. Rates arrive from module 2's machinery: the customer's list, the per-UoM rows, the Pricing Rules whose conditions the rows meet. For most quotations the pre-fill is the offer, and the preparer's job is verification, not composition: the right list resolved, the expected rule fired (the 50-unit row showing its break), the units matching the rates.

2. The deviation ladder. Negotiated business deviates — and deviations are decisions with owners, per the written ladder:

1. Within the sales function's band — deviations up to the policy's percentage on standard lines: applied by the preparer, reason noted on the document.
2. Within the manager's band — deeper deviations or sensitive lines: approved by the sales manager before issue, the approval recorded on the document (the site's approval mechanism or the documented note per the procedure).
3. Above the bands — owner approval, documented. Enterprise negotiations routinely live here, and the approval names the specific concession (the line, the rate, the condition), not a blanket permission.

The ladder mirrors the credit ladder (module 1) deliberately: prices and credit are the two areas where a sales document commits the business's money, and both move only with named approval.

3. Concessions are specific. A negotiated concession states its scope: which lines, what rate or percentage, tied to what (the volume, the bundle, the term). Scope matters at revision time (Chapter 4) and at order time (module 4): the concession granted on terminals does not silently spread to scanners in round two, because the approval named terminals. The document's rows and notes carry the scope; the approval file carries the decision.

4. Margin visibility. Where the role's view exposes valuation-based margin, the pre-issue read is standing procedure: the offer's gross margin per line and total against the policy floor. Deviations that breach the floor are exactly the cases the upper ladder bands exist for — the approval is the business deciding, with the arithmetic visible, that this offer is worth winning at this price. An offer issued below floor without that decision is Chapter 9's first error.

5. The deviations read — monthly. Quotations issued in the month with rates below list, listed with line, list rate, offered rate, band, and approver — reconciled against the ladder. The read is the pricing control's offer-side audit, the sibling of module 2's price changes read: list prices move by governed update; document prices deviate by laddered approval; and both leave monthly evidence.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Validity and revisions
lessons.html:
An issued offer binds the business while valid. This chapter is the validity discipline and the revision procedure.

1. Valid Till discipline.

1. Every quotation carries a validity date — the policy's standard window, shortened for volatile-cost lines (imported goods in a moving exchange environment carry the short window the policy names).
2. The offer is honoured within its validity — a customer accepting on the last valid day gets the quoted terms; that is what issuing a dated offer means, and the pricing of the offer accounts for the window's exposure.
3. Expired offers are not resurrected by editing — acceptance after expiry triggers a re-quote (a revision at current prices, Chapter 4.3), because the costs behind the offer have had time to move and the old document's arithmetic no longer states the business's position.

2. The no-silent-edit rule. A submitted, sent quotation is a record of what was offered. It is never edited in place to reflect a new round — the customer holds the old version, the business would hold a different one, and the negotiation would proceed from two disagreeing documents. Every change after issue is a revision.

3. The revision procedure. Per negotiation round:

1. The new version is created from the prior — amend or duplicate per the site's convention, carrying the reference to the version it supersedes, so the thread reads in order.
2. The changes are the round's changes only — the conceded lines at their approved rates, the adjusted quantities, the revised terms — each within its ladder approval (Chapter 3).
3. The superseded version is closed — marked per the convention so the pipeline reads (Chapter 6) count one live offer per negotiation, not one per round.
4. The new version issues with its own validity — the window restarts from the revision date.

4. The negotiation file. Enterprise negotiations produce a thread: versions, approvals, the customer's responses. The file — the versions in sequence, each approval against its round, the correspondence — is the negotiation's record, and it answers the two questions that always arrive later: what did we offer when, and who approved the movement. Module 4 consumes this file at order time: the order is checked against the final version, and the file is where any discrepancy is resolved from.

5. The validity read — weekly. Open quotations by days-to-expiry: offers expiring within the follow-up window get their Chapter 6 follow-up before the date; offers past expiry are closed as expired (or revived by deliberate re-quote), so the pipeline holds only live commitments. An open expired quotation is a misstated pipeline and a latent dispute — the read keeps both at zero.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Terms and the offer pack
lessons.html:
The offer is more than its rows. This chapter is the terms machinery and the pack the customer receives.

1. Terms and Conditions templates. Open Terms and Conditions (awesome bar) > New: named templates carrying the standing text — delivery terms, payment terms restated in words, warranty and support statements, the validity restatement, the legal boilerplate the business's counsel approved. The rules:

1. Templates are the only source of terms text — selected on the document, not typed per quotation. Typed terms are unreviewed terms, and unreviewed terms are what the business discovers it agreed to during a dispute.
2. Templates are owned — the register row names the owner (the owner or counsel for legal text) and the review date; changes are governed with effective dates.
3. Template per context — the standard trade template, the enterprise template with its support and training clauses, the tender template per the tender's requirements. The document selects the context's template; deviations for one negotiation are the negotiation file's documented exception, approved like any concession.

2. The offer pack. What the customer receives, assembled per the policy:

1. The quotation print — the document on the letterhead, per the print format the site standardises. The print is read before sending, as the customer will read it: rows, units, taxes, totals, validity, terms.
2. The attachments per context — specification sheets for equipment lines, the company profile for new prospects, the tender's required documents per its checklist.
3. The transmission record — the pack sends from the system (the email with the PDF) or is dispatched with its record; either way the file holds what was sent, to whom, when. The sent pack is the offer; the internal draft is not.

3. Print discipline.

1. One standard format per document type — the format the business's documents carry, maintained by the sysadmin lane; per-user format improvisation produces offers that look like different companies.
2. What prints is what the record says — no manual PDF editing after generation; a correction is a revision (Chapter 4), regenerated and re-sent.
3. The letterhead and registration details — current and correct per the compliance owner, because the offer is a business document carrying the business's legal identity.

4. The terms read — annually. With the pricing review: templates against their owners and review dates; the legal text reconfirmed or updated by counsel; superseded templates disabled; and a sample of the year's enterprise offers checked for typed-terms exceptions that should have been template updates.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The pipeline reads
lessons.html:
Open quotations are the sales pipeline's commitments. This chapter is the reads that keep the pipeline true and worked.

1. The open-quotations read — weekly. All open quotations, by age and days-to-validity:

1. The follow-up cadence — per the policy: the issue-week contact confirming receipt and questions; the mid-validity follow-up; the pre-expiry contact. Each contact notes on the document or its thread, so the negotiation file (Chapter 4) is complete and any colleague can pick up the thread.
2. The expiry hygiene — Chapter 4's read folded in: expiring offers followed up, expired offers closed.

2. Outcome marking. Every quotation ends in a state, marked when known:

1. Ordered — converted per Chapter 7; the system links the order.
2. Lost — marked with the lost reason from the reason code set (price, availability, specification, relationship, no decision), because a pipeline that only records wins cannot answer why it loses. Reason codes are a register set: few, defined, reviewed — free-text reasons aggregate into nothing.
3. Expired — the passive loss, closed by the weekly read.

3. The conversion read — monthly. Quotations issued, ordered, lost, and expired across the window; the conversion rate by count and by value; the lost reasons distribution. The read's uses, stated flatly:

1. The rate trend — a falling conversion rate is a pricing, availability, or follow-up question; the lost-reason distribution says which.
2. The value-weighted view — winning many small offers while losing the large ones reads differently from the count alone; both figures are compiled.
3. The aging tail — offers open beyond the standard cycle without outcome marks are follow-up failures or marking failures; the read lists them to zero.

4. The deviation-versus-outcome read — quarterly. The monthly deviations read (Chapter 3) joined to outcomes: what the conceded offers won, at what margin, against what the list-price offers won. The read is data for the owner's pricing review — whether the ladder's bands are calibrated, whether concessions are buying volume or merely spending margin — presented as figures with the offers named, per the standing data-not-editorial rule.

5. The pipeline's filing. The reads file with the sales function's records; the pipeline figures feed the sales page the owner reads monthly (the selling track's reporting is consolidated in module 7 alongside receivables); and the quotation file per negotiation remains the one-lookup answer for any offer's history.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Conversion to order
lessons.html:
A won quotation becomes a Sales Order. This chapter is the conversion procedure and its checks.

1. The conversion mechanics. From the accepted quotation: Create > Sales Order. The system carries the party, the rows, the rates, the taxes, and the terms into the order draft — this inheritance ensures the order states exactly what the customer accepted, without re-keying and without re-keying errors.

2. The conversion checks, in order.

1. The accepted version — the order is created from the final revision, verified against the negotiation file (Chapter 4). Creating from a superseded version ships the wrong round's prices; the file's version thread is the control against this.
2. Validity standing — acceptance within the validity window (Chapter 4's rule; expired acceptance re-quotes first).
3. The customer's standing — for prospects quoted as leads, the customer gate completes now (module 1): the record, the terms and credit per the ladder, before the order submits. For existing customers, the credit check runs at order submission per module 1's machinery — a won offer that exceeds the limit routes to the credit decision, not around it.
4. Acceptance evidence — the customer's acceptance (the signed offer, the purchase order document, the written confirmation) attaches to the order. The agreement's evidence lives with the commitment document, because module 4's delivery and invoicing disputes resolve from it.

3. Partial acceptance. The customer accepts part of the offer: the order carries the accepted rows only; the quotation's remaining rows stay open or close per the negotiation's reality (the declined lines marked lost with their reason; the deferred lines carried in a follow-on quotation with current validity). The order never carries rows the customer did not accept, and the quotation's outcome marking reflects what actually happened per line group.

4. Changes at acceptance. The customer accepts with one change — a quantity, a delivery split, a term. The change routes by size: within the ladder's bands, the order draft carries it with the approval noted; beyond them, a final revision issues and is accepted before the order proceeds. The rule is the same as everywhere in the module: the order states what was agreed, and what was agreed has its approval.

5. The handoff. The submitted order opens module 4's territory: the commitment schedule, the reservation of stock, the delivery planning. This module's contribution ends with a clean handoff — the order matching the final offer, the evidence attached, the quotation marked ordered and linked — and the negotiation file closed into the order's record.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: the BizRetail Ltd offer
lessons.html:
This chapter runs Chapters 2-7 through an enterprise negotiation: BizRetail Ltd, a chain requesting a POS hardware and setup offer for 12 branches — 12 terminals, 12 scanners, 12 printers — plus installation and training. The cycle runs three weeks and two rounds. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the request and the draft (Chapter 2). The request arrives from an onboarded customer (module 1's gate completed at relationship start). The quotation drafts from the registers: the equipment lines from the item register with their units, installation and training as the service lines the register carries, rates pre-filling from the Trade list. Validity set to the policy's enterprise window; the enterprise T&C template selected (support and training clauses standing). The margin view is read; the draft clears review at the value threshold and issues as round one — the offer pack: the print on letterhead, the equipment specification sheets attached, the transmission recorded.

Step 2 — round one's response (Chapters 3-4). BizRetail Ltd responds inside the validity window: the specification is accepted; the commercial ask is a concession on the terminal lines and a training restructure. The deviation routes per the ladder: the terminal concession sits above the manager's band and goes to the owner with the margin arithmetic — approved as a named, specific concession: the terminal lines at the conceded rate, tied to the 12-branch volume; scanners and printers stay at list, because the approval names terminals only.

Step 3 — round two issues (Chapter 4). The revision creates from round one, carrying the reference: the terminal rows at the approved concession, the training line restructured per the discussion, everything else unchanged. Round one closes as superseded; round two issues with fresh validity. The negotiation file now holds: two versions in sequence, the owner's approval against round two's concession, and the correspondence thread.

Step 4 — acceptance and conversion (Chapter 7). Acceptance arrives in week three, inside round two's validity, as BizRetail Ltd's purchase order document. The conversion runs its checks: the order creates from round two (the final version, verified against the file); the credit check passes at the customer's limit; the acceptance document attaches to the order. One change at acceptance — a delivery scheduling request — is a module 4 scheduling matter carrying no commercial movement, noted for the order's schedule rather than re-quoted.

Step 5 — the record closes (Chapters 6-7). The quotation marks Ordered with the order linked; the conversion read counts the win at value; the deviations read carries the terminal concession with its owner approval — the quarter's deviation-versus-outcome read will show what the concession bought. The negotiation is answerable from one file: two versions, one approval, the acceptance, the order. Module 4 opens with this order — the commitment, its schedule, and the delivery waves across the 12 branches.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in quotations, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the below-floor offer without a decision. Symptom: offers issued under the margin floor by composition rather than approval; concessions nobody authorised. Correction: the deviations read run, the ladder applied retroactively where defensible, the offers re-quoted where not. Prevention: pre-fill as the default, the ladder for every deviation, the margin read before issue.

Error 2 — the silently edited offer. Symptom: a sent quotation edited in place; the customer and the business holding disagreeing documents; the dispute conducted from two versions. Correction: the record reconstructed from the transmission file; a clean revision issued. Prevention: the no-silent-edit rule — every post-issue change is a referenced revision.

Error 3 — the immortal offer. Symptom: quotations without validity or expired ones honoured months later at stale prices; the pipeline full of dead offers. Correction: the validity read run, expired offers closed, resurrections re-quoted at current prices. Prevention: Valid Till on every offer and the weekly read.

Error 4 — the spreading concession. Symptom: a concession approved for one line appearing on others in the next round; approvals treated as blanket permissions. Correction: the revision corrected against the approval's named scope. Prevention: concessions specific — line, rate, condition — and revisions checked against the approval file.

Error 5 — typed terms. Symptom: per-quotation terms text; commitments counsel never reviewed; support obligations discovered at dispute. Correction: the offers sampled, exceptional terms escalated, templates updated where the exception was right. Prevention: templates as the only terms source, owned and reviewed.

Error 6 — the unmarked pipeline. Symptom: quotations without outcomes; conversion rates uncomputable; lost reasons unknown. Correction: the tail worked to zero with outcomes marked. Prevention: the weekly open read, the reason code set, and the monthly conversion read.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the Quotation walk including the header checks, the row discipline, and the pre-issue verification; apply the pre-fill-first rate discipline with the deviation ladder and specific concessions; operate validity and the revision procedure with the negotiation file; assemble the offer pack from owned templates with print discipline; run the pipeline reads — open, outcomes, conversion, deviation-versus-outcome; and convert with the four checks, partial acceptance, and the clean handoff.

Module rule 3: an issued offer is a record — built from the registers, deviating only by the ladder's named approvals, valid to its date, changed only by referenced revision, sent as the pack the file preserves, and converted to order only from the final accepted version with its evidence attached. Module 4 covers Sales Orders.
