taxes_invoicing.title: Selling 6 — Taxes, Pricing Rules & Invoicing
taxes_invoicing.desc: Taxes, pricing governance, and invoicing preparation in ZhiftERP: the Nigerian VAT context — the 7.5% rate, the output liability flow, exempt classes, and the e-invoicing rules; Sales Taxes and Charges Templates — row types, account heads, the standard set, and accountant-only maintenance; item tax templates on mixed documents with per-line computation and the refusal rule; inclusive and exclusive pricing arithmetic with the one-posture-per-channel policy; discounts governance — the three instruments, their holders, the additional discount field, and the monthly read; and the watching reports — the trend read, the sales register, and the fifteen-minute five-check weekly habit feeding the monthly commercial review.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Taxes and invoicing preparation: scope and position
lessons.html:
This module covers the sales tax machinery, pricing and discount governance, and the preparation the Sales Invoice depends on. On completing this module you will be able to: state the Nigerian VAT context a selling configuration operates in; build and read Sales Taxes and Charges Templates; operate item tax templates on mixed documents; apply the inclusive and exclusive pricing postures correctly; govern the three discount instruments; and run the weekly watching reports.

Position on the document timeline. The selling documents post their effects in a fixed sequence: the Sales Order reserves stock (module 4), the Delivery Note deducts stock and posts cost (module 5), and the Sales Invoice posts revenue, tax, and the receivable (module 7). This module prepares the third step: the tax computation, the pricing integrity, and the reads that confirm both, so that invoicing in module 7 is an execution task rather than a correction task. Each preparation area below has its own chapter, its own custody assignment, and its own confirming read on a stated cadence.

What must be true before invoicing. The pre-invoicing state this module establishes:

1. The tax templates exist and are selected correctly — the document-level template (Chapter 3) and the item-level treatments (Chapter 4) together compute the tax the return will declare.
2. The pricing posture is consistent — inclusive or exclusive per channel by policy (Chapter 5), matching what was quoted (module 3's rule that the offer's tax total is the invoice's tax total).
3. Discounts carry their approvals — every departure from list price is one of the three governed instruments (Chapter 6).
4. The delivered quantities are known — module 5's %delivered figures state what is billable per the payment schedule.

Custody. The accountant owns the tax configuration and rulings — templates, account heads, item classifications, and the return itself; the sales function selects the decided templates and operates within them; and the standing rule for the module: tax on a document is computed by configuration, never edited by hand.

Module contents. Chapter 2: VAT in Nigeria. Chapter 3: Sales Taxes and Charges Templates. Chapter 4: item tax templates on documents. Chapter 5: inclusive and exclusive pricing. Chapter 6: discounts governance. Chapter 7: the watching reports. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — VAT in Nigeria
lessons.html:
The tax the selling configuration computes most often is Value Added Tax. This chapter states the context.

1. Output VAT. Nigerian VAT stands at 7.5%. When the business sells taxable goods or services, it charges VAT on the sale — added on top of the net price (exclusive) or contained within the shelf price (inclusive; Chapter 5 covers both arithmetics). The amount charged is not the business's revenue: it is collected on behalf of the government, held as a liability, and remitted with the periodic VAT return.

2. The liability flow. The accounting path every charged naira of VAT follows:

1. At invoicing — the tax row posts to the VAT output liability account (the account head the template names; Chapter 3).
2. Through the period — the liability account accumulates the VAT charged on all sales.
3. At the return — the accountant computes the period's position (output VAT less recoverable input VAT from the purchasing side, per the Procurement and Accounts tracks) and remits per the filing calendar.

The selling function's obligation in this flow is accuracy at step 1: the correct rate, on the correct base, posted to the correct account, on every document — because the return declares what the documents computed.

3. Exempt and zero-rated classes. Not all goods carry the standard rate. Nigerian VAT legislation exempts defined classes — including many pharmaceutical products, the class most relevant to the standing case — and zero-rates others. The operational consequences:

1. The item's treatment is stated on the item side (module 2, Chapter 7): the classification per the accountant's ruling table, applied at the item gate.
2. Mixed documents compute per line (Chapter 4): exempt rows at their treatment, standard rows at 7.5%, on one invoice.
3. Treatment changes are the accountant's dated rulings, never operator edits — the audit trail of a tax classification is examined in every tax audit.

4. The e-invoicing context. Where the business operates under the FIRS e-invoicing regime, submitted Sales Invoices transmit to the tax authority through the site's e-invoicing integration per the compliance configuration. The operational rules this adds: invoices carry the customer's TIN (module 1's gate requirement), the item and tax data must be complete and correct at submission because the transmitted document is the declared document, and corrections follow the credit-note lane (module 7) rather than deletion — the transmitted record is permanent.

5. The boundary. The accountant rules on taxability, rates, and the return; this module's chapters equip the selling function to configure and operate what the accountant has ruled. A tax question arising on a document — an unfamiliar class, a customer claiming exemption — routes to the accountant and waits for the ruling, per the standing rule from module 2.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Sales Taxes and Charges Templates
lessons.html:
The document-level tax computation is configured as a template. This chapter is the doctype and its maintenance.

1. The template record. Open Sales Taxes and Charges Template (awesome bar) > New: a named, ordered set of rows, each computing one charge. Documents select a template; the template's rows compute the document's tax section.

2. Row anatomy. Each row carries:

1. Type — the computation base:
  — On Net Total: a percentage of the document's net total — the standard base for VAT.
  — Actual: a fixed amount — used for flat charges such as a delivery fee.
  — On Previous Row Amount / On Previous Row Total: a percentage computed on an earlier row's result — used where a charge compounds on another charge; rare in the standing configuration and used only by the accountant's design.
2. Account Head — the ledger account the row posts to: the VAT output liability for the VAT row; the freight recovery account for a delivery charge. The account head is the connection between the document and the return, and it is the accountant's field.
3. Rate or Amount — 7.5 for the standard VAT row; the fixed figure for an Actual row.
4. Description — the text that prints on the document's tax section.

3. The standing template set. Per the site's design:

1. The standard VAT template — one row: VAT, On Net Total, 7.5%, posting to the VAT output liability. Set as the default so documents carry it unless a decided exception applies.
2. Variants only by decision — a delivery-charge variant (the VAT row plus an Actual freight row) for routes that bill freight; an export or zero-rated template where the business has such trade, per the accountant's ruling. Each variant is a register entry with its purpose; template proliferation is avoided for the same reason as price-list proliferation — every template is configuration to maintain and an opportunity to select wrongly.

4. Maintenance. Templates are created and changed by the accountant (or by the configuration role at the accountant's written instruction): a statutory rate change, a new account head, a new variant — each a governed, dated change. Template-write permission is held per the matrix; the selling function selects templates and reads their results, and does not edit their rows.

5. Reading a document's tax section. The verification habit: the tax section of any document shows the template's rows with their computed amounts. The reader confirms: the expected template name, the rate against the base (7.5% of the net total the rows show), and the total consistent with the pricing posture (Chapter 5). A tax section that cannot be read back to its template and rate is a configuration question to resolve before the document proceeds.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Item tax templates on documents
lessons.html:
Module 2, Chapter 7 set each item's tax classification. This chapter is the document-side arithmetic: how mixed taxability computes on one invoice.

1. The override mechanics. An Item Tax Template attaches to an item (or derives from its item group) and overrides the document template's rate for that row only:

1. The document template states VAT 7.5% On Net Total.
2. The exempt item's template states VAT 0% for the same account head.
3. On the document, the standard rows compute at 7.5%; the exempt rows compute at 0%; the tax section totals the per-line results.

The design means one document serves any basket: the pharmacy invoice carrying exempt medicines and standard-rated consumables computes each class correctly without splitting the sale across documents or editing any rate by hand.

2. What the operator sees and verifies. On a mixed document:

1. Per-line tax detail — the item-wise tax breakup (the document's tax detail view) shows each row's rate and amount: the exempt rows at zero, the standard rows at 7.5%.
2. The verification read — for any unfamiliar mix, the reader confirms a sample line of each class against the ruling table: the exempt item computing at zero because its template says so, not because someone edited the row.
3. The refusal rule — a line computing at an unexpected rate is a classification question (the item's template wrong or missing), resolved at the item record through the accountant's lane; the document is not corrected by hand because the next document would repeat the error.

3. The interaction with the document template. The two levels divide the work: the document template states the context's charges (VAT, and any freight or context charges); the item template states each product's treatment within that context. Selecting a different document template does not change an item's classification, and an item's classification applies on every document template that carries the account head. The division means each fact is stated once — the context on the document, the treatment on the item — per the standing one-source pattern.

4. The classification read, restated. The quarterly item tax read (module 2, Chapter 7) is the register-side control; this chapter adds the document-side sample: a monthly draw of mixed invoices checked line-by-line against the ruling table, riding the accountant's period close. Together the two reads confirm that what the register states and what the documents compute agree — which is the condition the VAT return depends on.

5. Zero-rated versus exempt, operationally. The accountant's distinction (zero-rated sales are taxable at 0% with input recovery; exempt sales are outside the charge with input restrictions) determines the return's treatment, not the document operator's procedure: both classes reach the document as item templates computing zero on the line. The operator's obligation is the same in both cases — the correct template on the item, verified, never hand-edited — and the return-side difference is the accountant's territory.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Inclusive and exclusive pricing
lessons.html:
One setting separates two pricing arithmetics. This chapter states both and the policy that governs them.

1. Exclusive pricing (the default). The entered rate is the net price; tax adds on top:

1. Rate ₦1,000, VAT 7.5% → tax ₦75, total ₦1,075.
2. The document shows net ₦1,000, VAT ₦75, gross ₦1,075.
3. This is the business-to-business posture: trade customers, procurement offices, and input-credit accounting work in net prices, and the Trade price list carries net rates.

2. Inclusive pricing. The entered rate already contains the tax; the system extracts it:

1. Rate ₦1,075 inclusive, VAT 7.5% → net ₦1,000, tax ₦75, total ₦1,075.
2. The extraction divides by (1 + rate): ₦1,075 ÷ 1.075 = ₦1,000 net.
3. This is the retail posture: shelf and counter prices are the prices customers pay, and the retail price list carries inclusive rates with the inclusive setting on the tax row.

3. The policy rule. The posture is set per channel by written policy — the retail list inclusive, the trade list exclusive — configured once in the price lists and templates, and never mixed ad hoc:

1. Confusing the postures misstates either the price or the VAT. An inclusive rate entered where the system expects exclusive charges the customer 7.5% over the intended price; an exclusive rate entered as inclusive under-declares the VAT by the same proportion.
2. The quotation-to-invoice consistency rule (module 3) depends on the posture holding constant through the document chain: what was quoted at a posture invoices at that posture.
3. Posture changes are configuration decisions — a channel moving from one posture to the other is a governed change with the price lists re-based arithmetically and the change dated, because every price on the list means something different after the switch.

4. Rounding. The document computes line and total rounding per the site's rounding configuration; the rounded figures are the document's figures. The operational rule: rounding differences are configuration matters for the accountant, not amounts to be adjusted by editing a tax row — a tax section is never hand-balanced.

5. Reading a priced document. The check that closes the chapter: given any document, the reader states its posture (from the list and template), confirms the arithmetic in the correct direction (net plus tax, or gross containing tax), and confirms the totals match the customer's expectation for the channel. The three-line check takes under a minute and precedes any conversation about a total a customer disputes.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Discounts governance
lessons.html:
Three instruments reduce a price below list. This chapter assigns each its holder and its record, consolidating the controls the track has built.

1. The three instruments and their holders.

1. The price list (module 2) — the standing class price, maintained by the pricing function through the governed update. A class that always pays less has a list (or a list-derived arrangement), not a permanent discount entered per document.
2. The Pricing Rule (module 2, Chapter 6) — the standing condition: quantity breaks, promotions, class discounts — registered, owned, dated, firing by configuration. Policy that repeats belongs here, so that it applies uniformly and expires on its date.
3. The document-level concession — the row rate edit, the row discount percentage, and the additional discount field on the document total: the negotiator's instruments for genuine one-case concessions, governed by the deviation ladder (module 3) at quotation time and by the amendment taxonomy (module 4) after commitment.

2. The assignment rule. Each price departure uses the instrument that matches its nature: standing class pricing in lists; repeating conditions in rules; one-case concessions on documents with their approvals. Misassignment is the governance failure the reads detect — the repeating document discount that should be a rule (the same customer conceded the same percentage monthly by hand), or the rule created for one negotiation that should have been a document concession with an approval.

3. The additional discount field. The document-total discount (percentage or amount, applied on net or gross per configuration) is the broadest instrument and carries the tightest governance: permitted roles per the matrix, the ladder band by size, the reason on the document, and visibility in the discounts read. Its legitimate uses are whole-document commercial decisions (the negotiated package discount); its illegitimate use is as a convenience field that hides per-line pricing from the record.

4. Visibility. Every instrument leaves its price visible against list:

1. The document shows the price list rate and the transacted rate per row; the difference is the concession, readable per line.
2. Rule effects are attributable — the applied rule is identifiable on the row's pricing detail.
3. The discounts read (below) aggregates the differences.

5. The discounts read — monthly. The month's documents with transacted rates below list, grouped by instrument, customer, and approver: list-versus-transacted value by customer group (the standing concession pattern that should become a rule or a list), document concessions against their ladder approvals (the module 3 read continued through orders and invoices), and additional-discount usage by role. The read files with the pricing review, and its output is the owner's data for recalibrating lists, rules, and bands.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The watching reports
lessons.html:
Configuration is confirmed by reading. This chapter is the weekly reporting habit and the reads it comprises.

1. Sales Analytics — the movement view. Revenue cut by customer, item, item group, customer group, or territory, across time periods — the dimensions the track's registers disciplined (modules 1-2) are the dimensions this report can cut by. The standing read is the trend read: the current period against the prior periods on each major dimension. A movement of the order of 30% across three periods on any dimension — a customer's volume, a group's revenue, a territory's mix — is a change to investigate and explain, not a figure to note: the explanation (a gained or lost account, a price change, a stock gap, a seasonal pattern) is written into the week's note so the following reader inherits it.

2. The sales register — the tax view. The period's invoices with their taxable values and tax amounts by rate class: the figures the VAT return will declare. The weekly pass confirms the period is accumulating correctly — standard-rated value at 7.5%, exempt value at zero, the split consistent with the business's mix — so the return at period end is a compilation, not an investigation. Anomalies (an exempt-class item accumulating standard-rated tax) route to the classification lane at the item record.

3. The execution reads, consolidated. The track's weekly reads meet here as one screen sequence: open quotations by validity (module 3), overdue and at-risk order rows (module 4), delivered-not-billed (module 5), pending acknowledgments (module 5), and the discounts summary (Chapter 6). Each has its own procedure in its own module; the habit this chapter adds is the consolidated pass.

4. The fifteen-minute five-check read — weekly. The consolidated pass, as a fixed procedure:

1. Open quotations — expiring offers followed up; expired ones closed.
2. Overdue order rows — each with owner and action.
3. Delivered-not-billed — the list that must clear at the invoicing run.
4. The discounts summary — concessions against approvals.
5. The trend read — the analytics pass with its written explanations.

The five checks take approximately fifteen minutes on a maintained book, and the output is a short written note: the exceptions, their owners, their actions. The note files with the sales records; the month's four notes are the material of the monthly commercial review.

5. The monthly commercial review. The owner's session, fed by the weekly notes and the monthly reads (conversion, deviations, discounts, returns): the book's state, the pipeline's state, the pricing controls' evidence, and the decisions — list updates, rule changes, band recalibrations — each entering the governed lanes the track has defined. The review closes the loop this module opened: configuration, operation, reading, adjustment.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: HealthTrade's tax and pricing layer
lessons.html:
This chapter applies Chapters 2-7 to the standing case. Configuration values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the VAT spine (Chapters 2-3). One standard template: VAT, On Net Total, 7.5%, posting to the VAT output liability account the accountant confirmed; set as the default template. One variant by decision: the delivery-charge template — the VAT row plus an Actual freight row posting to freight recovery — for the routes that bill freight. Both entered in the configuration register with their purposes; template-write permission confirmed as the accountant's role only.

Step 2 — the item treatments (Chapter 4). The ruling table applies by class: the exempt pharmaceutical classes carry the 0% item tax template; consumables and equipment carry standard treatment. The mixed-basket verification draft — exempt medicines and standard consumables on one document — computes per line: exempt rows at zero, standard rows at 7.5%, the item-wise breakup readable. The draft is deleted after reading; the sample files with the quarter's classification read.

Step 3 — the postures (Chapter 5). By written policy: the retail channel prices inclusive — counter prices are what customers pay, the Standard Selling list carries inclusive rates, and the inclusive setting is on; the trade channel prices exclusive — the Trade list carries net rates, and BizRetail Ltd's documents show net, VAT, and gross separately (the arithmetic their procurement office reconciles: net ₦1,000-per-unit lines carrying ₦75 VAT to ₦1,075 gross). The posture check joins the pre-issue verification on both channels.

Step 4 — discounts assigned to instruments (Chapter 6). The audit of existing practice moves each case to its instrument: the chain pricing that was being conceded per document moves to the Trade list where it belongs; the volume break stands as the registered Pricing Rule (module 2's ₦950-from-50-units); one-case concessions remain document concessions with ladder approvals — the BizRetail terminal concession the standing example. The additional discount field's permission narrows to the roles the matrix names.

Step 5 — the weekly habit installed (Chapter 7). The five-check read runs its first weeks: the trend read explains a 30% movement across three periods in one territory (a chain's new branches concentrating volume — the explanation written into the note); the sales register accumulates the period's split (standard-rated consumables, exempt pharmaceuticals) ready for the return; delivered-not-billed clears at each invoicing run. The weekly notes file; the first monthly commercial review works from four notes and the monthly reads, and its decisions — one list correction, one rule end-dated — enter the governed lanes.

The layer's evidence. The configuration register holds the templates and their purposes; the ruling table and classification reads hold the treatments; the policy holds the postures; the discounts read holds the concession evidence; the weekly notes hold the reading habit. The tax and pricing layer is answerable end to end — from any document's tax row back to its template, rate, and account, and from any transacted price back to its instrument and approval.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in tax and pricing operation, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the hand-edited tax row. Symptom: tax amounts adjusted on documents to match expectations; the return disagreeing with the configuration; rounding differences balanced by edits. Correction: the affected documents corrected through the proper lanes; the configuration question resolved at the template. Prevention: tax computed by configuration only, and template-write permission held per the matrix.

Error 2 — the misclassified line. Symptom: an exempt item computing at 7.5% or a standard item at zero; the document corrected by hand so the next document repeats the error. Correction: the item's template fixed through the accountant's lane; affected documents corrected. Prevention: the refusal rule — classification questions resolve at the item record — and the two classification reads.

Error 3 — the mixed posture. Symptom: inclusive rates entered on the exclusive channel or the reverse; prices 7.5% adrift or VAT under-declared. Correction: the affected list re-based arithmetically as a governed change. Prevention: one posture per channel by written policy, configured once, checked in the pre-issue read.

Error 4 — the instrument misassigned. Symptom: the same discount conceded per document monthly by hand; rules created for single negotiations; the additional discount field used to hide line pricing. Correction: each standing case moved to its instrument — list, rule, or approved concession. Prevention: the assignment rule and the monthly discounts read.

Error 5 — the unread configuration. Symptom: templates, treatments, and postures assumed correct because they were set correctly once; drift discovered at the return. Correction: the reads run and the findings fixed at their sources. Prevention: the weekly register pass, the monthly document sample, and the quarterly classification read.

Error 6 — the unexplained trend. Symptom: analytics read but movements unexplained; the 30% shift noticed at quarter end with its cause cold. Correction: the investigation run late and the explanation recorded. Prevention: the trend read weekly with explanations written into the note.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the VAT context — the 7.5% rate, the liability flow, exempt classes, and the e-invoicing rules; build and read a template — row types, account heads, the standard set; operate item tax templates on mixed documents with the refusal rule; apply both pricing arithmetics and the one-posture-per-channel policy; assign every discount to its instrument with its holder and record; and run the fifteen-minute five-check read with the trend explanations.

Module rule 6: tax on a document is computed by configuration — the accountant's templates and treatments, selected not edited, at the channel's declared posture — and every price below list is one of three governed instruments with its record; the weekly reads confirm both before the invoice declares them. Module 7 covers the Sales Invoice, payments, and collections.

sales_invoice.title: Selling 7 — The Sales Invoice, Payments & Collections
sales_invoice.desc: The Sales Invoice, payments, and collections in ZhiftERP: the field walk — template due dates, honest posting dates, rates from the agreement, per-row references, and advance allocation at preparation; the three creation paths — from the Delivery Note for performance, from the Sales Order for the schedule, direct only per policy — and the run's two worklists; the four postings of submission with the e-invoicing rules and the three correction lanes; Payment Entries with remittance-led allocation, partial payments, short-pay routing, and the weekly unallocated read; credit notes — the return tie, value-only exceptions, credit-or-refund settlement; the receivables aging, statement cycle, and dunning configuration; and the four-gear collections procedure from the 7-day pre-due contact to the resolution decision.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Sales Invoice: scope and position
lessons.html:
This module covers the Sales Invoice, payments, credit notes, receivables, and collections in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: complete the Sales Invoice field walk; use the correct creation path for each billing basis; state what submission posts; record and allocate Payment Entries including advances; issue credit notes through the return tie; run the receivables and statement cycle; and operate the four-gear collections procedure.

What a Sales Invoice is. The Sales Invoice is the accounting event of the sale: it posts the revenue, the output VAT, and the receivable. On the document timeline (module 6, Chapter 1) it is the third posting — the order reserved, the delivery deducted stock and posted cost, and the invoice now claims the money. From submission, the customer owes the invoiced amount on the due date the terms compute, and the receivables machinery tracks it until it is paid, credited, or escalated.

Position and dependencies. The invoice draws on everything the track has built:

1. The customer record (module 1) — the payer, the terms template, the TIN the e-invoicing regime requires.
2. The pricing and tax layer (modules 2, 6) — rates from the order's agreement; tax computed by configuration at the channel's posture.
3. The order and its schedule (module 4) — what is billable, per the payment schedule and the delivered state.
4. The deliveries (module 5) — the %delivered figures and the delivered-not-billed list the invoicing run clears.

The invoicing run. Invoicing operates on a cadence per the policy — the standing pattern is a scheduled run (daily or twice-weekly per volume) that works the delivered-not-billed list and the due milestones to zero, plus immediate invoicing where the flow requires it (counter sales, cash-and-carry). A sale delivered but unbilled is performance without a claim; the run's discipline keeps that interval short and measured.

Custody. The invoicing role prepares and submits invoices per the matrix; the accounts function owns the receivable, the allocation of money, and the statements; collections operate per the written procedure (Chapter 8); and the standing rule: every invoice states what the order agreed and the delivery performed — billed from the documents, due by the template, and tracked to its settlement.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the field walk. Chapter 3: creation paths. Chapter 4: what submission posts. Chapter 5: Payment Entries and allocation. Chapter 6: credit notes. Chapter 7: receivables and statements. Chapter 8: collections. Chapter 9: worked example. Chapter 10: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Sales Invoice doctype
lessons.html:
Create the Sales Invoice from its source document (Chapter 3 covers the paths). Complete or verify the fields in order.

1. Customer and header. The customer carries from the source with the terms template, currency, and billing address. The TIN presence check applies where e-invoicing operates — a customer record missing its TIN is corrected at the record (module 1's gate requirement) before the invoice submits.

2. Posting Date and Due Date. The posting date is the invoice date — the date the revenue and receivable post, set honestly per the standing date rule. The due date computes from the payment terms template (module 1, Chapter 5): the schedule rows generate per the template's portions and intervals. Due dates are never typed over — the receivables aging computes from them, and a typed date detaches the invoice from the terms decision.

3. The items table. Rows draw from the source document:

1. Quantities — the billed quantities per the basis: delivered quantities when billing from deliveries; the milestone's portion when billing the schedule.
2. Rates — carried from the order's agreement; the invoice does not renegotiate. A rate correction at invoice time is an order amendment first (module 4's taxonomy), then a re-draw.
3. References — the Sales Order and Delivery Note links per row: the references connect the claim to the agreement and the performance, and every reconciliation and dispute works through them.

4. Taxes. The template and item treatments compute per module 6 — read, not edited. The item-wise breakup on a mixed invoice is verified against the ruling table on the sample cadence.

5. The payment schedule section. On milestone orders, the invoice's schedule rows reflect the portion being claimed (Chapter 3.3); on standing-terms invoices, the single row at the template's interval.

6. Advance allocation. Where advances exist against the order (module 4, Chapter 6), the allocation section applies them against this invoice — Chapter 5 covers the mechanics. The rule at entry: the allocation is part of preparing the invoice, not a later cleanup.

7. Save, review, submit. Draft review per the value threshold; submission posts the accounting event (Chapter 4) and, under the e-invoicing regime, transmits the document (module 6, Chapter 2's rules: the transmitted record is permanent; corrections follow the credit-note lane).

Verification per invoice. The customer and terms correct; the posting date honest; quantities per the basis; rates per the agreement; references present; taxes read back to template and treatment; advances allocated; then submit on the run's cadence.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Creation paths and billing bases
lessons.html:
An invoice is created from its billing basis. This chapter is the three paths and when each applies.

1. From the Delivery Note — billing performance. The standard trade path: Create > Sales Invoice from the Delivery Note (or from several notes consolidated per the policy). The invoice draws the delivered rows and quantities; %billed advances against the order; the delivered-not-billed list clears. This path bills exactly what shipped, and the row references carry both documents.

2. From the Sales Order — billing the schedule. The milestone path: Create > Sales Invoice from the order, drawing the portion the payment schedule makes due — the advance portion at order (where the terms bill the advance as an invoice per the site's configuration), the delivery portion when its wave ships, the retention at completion. The invoice's rows and schedule section state the portion claimed; the order's %billed tracks the cumulative claim against the total. Milestone billing follows the schedule as written — the module 4 milestone read exists to catch portions that fell between runs.

3. Direct invoices — policy-limited. Invoices without a source document are confined to the cases the policy names (counter sales through the POS flow, defined service charges): each carries its own complete data and its policy reference. A direct invoice for what should have been an order-and-delivery flow bypasses reservation, fulfilment tracking, and the document chain — the monthly invoice sample (Chapter 7) lists direct invoices against the policy's cases.

4. Choosing the path. The decision is mechanical: bill performance from the Delivery Note; bill the schedule from the Sales Order; bill nothing directly except the policy's named cases. Mixed situations resolve by their parts — the delivered wave bills from its notes while the milestone structure governs how much of the value is claimable now; the site's configuration (deduct advances, percentage billing) implements the arithmetic, and the order file shows the claim's build-up.

5. Consolidation and splitting. Per the policy: multiple deliveries to one customer may consolidate onto one invoice within a period (fewer documents for the customer's payables to process); one delivery never splits across invoices without a schedule reason (partial claims create allocation complexity with no operational gain). Consolidated invoices keep per-row references so each line traces to its delivery.

6. The run's worklist. Each invoicing run works two lists to zero: the delivered-not-billed list (path 1) and the due-milestones list (path 2). Both lists come from the track's standing reads; the run's output — invoices submitted, exceptions carried with reasons — files with the run per the one-lookup standard.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — What submission posts
lessons.html:
Submission converts the verified draft into the accounting event. This chapter states each posting and its consequence.

1. The receivable. The customer's account (the receivables control through the customer ledger) debits for the gross total: the customer now owes the invoice on its due date. The customer's outstanding balance — the figure the credit limit checks against (module 1) — increases accordingly.

2. The revenue. The income accounts credit per the item defaults (module 2's sales defaults, per the accountant's design): the sale's revenue is recognised on the posting date. Where cost posted at delivery (module 5), the margin for the period reads from the two documents together — cost at despatch, revenue at invoice — and the delivered-not-billed interval is the timing gap between them.

3. The tax. The VAT rows credit the output liability account per the template (module 6): the period's return accumulates. Under e-invoicing, submission also transmits the document per the compliance configuration — the fiscal record and the ledger record are created by the same act, and both are permanent.

4. The order update. %billed advances on the linked order; the milestone rows mark as claimed; the order's status moves per the vocabulary when billing completes.

5. Corrections after submission. The lanes, matching what the error is:

1. The invoice claims what did not happen (wrong quantities, wrong customer, duplicate): under e-invoicing the correction is a credit note reversing the claim plus a correct re-invoice — the transmitted record is never deleted. Outside the regime, same-day cancellation with reason is permitted per the document rules; the credit-note lane remains the standard where any doubt exists.
2. The claim is right but the money side changes (returned goods, agreed price adjustment after the fact): the credit note lane (Chapter 6), sized to the change, referenced to the invoice.
3. A field error with no accounting effect (a reference, a description): the administrative note per the document rules.

6. The GL tie. The invoice's postings participate in the accounts function's controls: the receivables control account reconciles to the customer ledger, the revenue accounts reconcile to the sales register (module 6, Chapter 7), and the VAT accumulation reconciles to the return. An invoicing function that keeps its documents clean — honest dates, template-computed tax, referenced rows — is what makes those reconciliations arithmetic rather than investigation.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Payment Entries and allocation
lessons.html:
Money arrives and must land on the right claims. This chapter is the Payment Entry and the allocation discipline.

1. The Payment Entry. Open Payment Entry (awesome bar) > New (or Create > Payment from the invoice): the party, the payment type (Receive), the amounts, the bank or cash account the money entered, the date, and the reference (the customer's transfer reference or instrument number). The entry records that money arrived; the allocation section records what it pays.

2. Allocation. The allocation table lists the customer's open invoices; the received amount allocates against them:

1. Per the customer's remittance advice — the customer states which invoices the payment covers; the allocation follows their statement, because the customer's ledger and the business's must agree invoice-by-invoice.
2. Partial payments — an invoice may allocate partially; the balance remains outstanding at its due date and ages accordingly.
3. Unallocated amounts — money received without identifiable invoices posts as unallocated (advance) against the customer and is resolved through the weekly unallocated read: the remittance chased, the allocation completed. A ledger carrying old unallocated amounts and old open invoices side by side is one reconciliation behind on every statement it sends.

3. Advance allocation. The order advance (module 4, Chapter 6) allocates when its invoices raise:

1. The milestone invoice prepares with its allocation section drawing the order's advance.
2. The advance applies per the schedule's arithmetic — the advance portion offsets the claims it funded, in order, until consumed.
3. The customer's statement then reads coherently: the order, the advance received, the invoices, the allocations, the balances due at their dates.

4. Payment discipline.

1. Same-day recording — payments record on the day they are identified in the bank, at the amount received; the receivables position is only as current as the last recorded payment.
2. No netting by hand — deductions the customer takes (a disputed line, a claimed rebate) are not absorbed by under-allocating silently: the short-pay records as a partial allocation and the difference routes to its lane — the credit note if the deduction is agreed, the dispute procedure if not.
3. Reconciliation — the bank reconciliation (the Accounts track) confirms that recorded payments match bank movements; the selling-side obligation is entries that are complete, dated, and referenced.

5. The allocation reads. Weekly: unallocated receipts by age, worked to zero; invoices with partial allocations, confirmed against remittances. Monthly: the allocation sample — payments traced from bank line to entry to invoice — riding the accounts function's close.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Credit notes
lessons.html:
The claim reduces when goods return or terms adjust. This chapter is the credit note lane.

1. The credit note. A Sales Invoice marked as a return (Is Return), created against the original invoice so the reference carries. It posts the reverse of Chapter 4: the receivable credits (the customer owes less), revenue debits, and the VAT output reverses for the credited value — the return's tax leaves the period's accumulation, which is what keeps the VAT return aligned with the commercial reality.

2. The return tie. The standing case is module 5's return lane completing its money side:

1. The return Delivery Note recorded what came back (quantities, identities, condition).
2. The credit note issues against the original invoice for the returned quantities at their invoiced rates — the two documents referenced to each other.
3. The rule from module 5 restated: the stock document records what came back; the credit document records what is owed for it — the credit note never issues without its physical return where goods are involved, and the return read lists credit notes against their return documents.

3. Non-return credits. Price adjustments agreed after invoicing (a billing error, a negotiated settlement of a dispute) issue as credit notes without stock rows — value-only credits with the reason and the approval per the ladder band the adjustment belongs to. These are the exception lane, listed monthly with approvers, because a value credit is a price change after the fact and carries the same governance as any other price movement.

4. Credit or refund. The credit note creates a balance in the customer's favour. Its settlement:

1. Allocation against open or future invoices — the standard case for trading relationships: the credit offsets what the customer owes or will owe.
2. Refund — a Payment Entry (Pay) returning money, per the policy's authorisation: refunds move cash and carry the tighter approval.
3. The choice records with the credit; a credit note left unsettled and unallocated ages on the ledger like any open item and appears in the weekly read.

5. E-invoicing and credit notes. Under the regime, credit notes transmit like invoices and reference the fiscal record they adjust. The operational consequences: the credit note's data completeness matters at submission (the reference to the original, the reason coding per the configuration), and the invoice-plus-credit pair is the permanent public record of the correction — the reason the standing rule prefers the credit lane even where cancellation is technically available.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Receivables and statements
lessons.html:
Open invoices age until they are paid. This chapter is the receivables view and the statement cycle.

1. The receivables aging. The Accounts Receivable report: open invoices per customer, bucketed by age against due date (current, then the aging buckets per the site's configuration). The figures the report depends on are the ones this track disciplined: due dates from templates (module 1), invoices from documents (Chapters 2-3), payments allocated (Chapter 5), credits settled (Chapter 6). The aging is read weekly by the collections function and monthly by the owner with the receivables summary.

2. Reading the aging. The standing reads on the report:

1. The overdue concentration — overdue value by customer, largest first: the collections worklist (Chapter 8).
2. The bucket drift — value moving rightward across buckets between reads: an account drifting from current to 30-plus is engaged at the drift, not at the write-off conversation.
3. The integrity anomalies — negative lines (unallocated credits or payments sitting beside open invoices), old partial balances, disputed lines flagged per the dispute procedure: each routes to its lane — allocation, credit settlement, or the dispute file.

3. The statement cycle. The Statement of Accounts per customer (module 1, Chapter 5) sends on the monthly cadence to the named accounts payable contact, and on demand at collection conversations:

1. The statement lists invoices, credits, payments, allocations, and the balance by due date — the customer's copy of the ledger.
2. Statement disputes are findings: a customer's ledger disagreeing with the statement traces through the references (invoice to delivery to order) and resolves at the document that differs; recurring disagreement with one customer indicates an allocation or documentation gap on one side, located through the monthly reconciliation of that account.
3. The statement is the collections procedure's second gear (Chapter 8); its regularity is what makes the overdue conversation a follow-up rather than a surprise.

4. Dunning configuration. Where the site uses the system's reminder machinery, the reminder templates and cadence are configured per the collections procedure — the letters state facts from the ledger (invoices, dates, amounts) in the firm's standard wording, and every sent reminder records against the customer. Automation serves the procedure; the gears and their decisions remain Chapter 8's owned steps.

5. The receivables summary — monthly. The owner's view: total receivables, overdue value and percentage, DSO or collection-days per the accountant's measure, the top overdue accounts with their gear status, credits outstanding, unallocated cash. One page, from the reads above, filed with the month's commercial review (module 6, Chapter 7).

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Collections: the four-gear procedure
lessons.html:
Collections run as a written procedure with four gears, each with its trigger, its action, and its record. Every contact records against the customer with date, person, and outcome — the collections file is part of the account's record.

1. Gear one — the pre-due contact. Trigger: an invoice above the policy's value threshold reaches 7 days before due. Action: the courtesy contact to the accounts payable contact — the invoice is with them, complete, approved for payment, and any query is surfaced now. Purpose: queries and missing-document problems are resolved before the due date instead of becoming the reason for lateness after it. The pre-due read lists the week's qualifying invoices; the contacts record.

2. Gear two — the statement at due. Trigger: the due date passes without payment. Action: the statement (Chapter 7) with the due items marked, sent to the named contact with the standard covering note. Purpose: the formal record that the balance is due, in the customer's payables process, referenced for every later step.

3. Gear three — the overdue ladder. Trigger: the policy's overdue intervals. Action, stepped:

1. The first reminder at the first interval — the reminder letter with the ledger facts; the call to the contact; the outcome recorded (a promise-to-pay date enters the file and is followed up on that date).
2. The escalated reminder at the second interval — the firmer standard letter; the conversation moves up a level on both sides per the procedure.
3. The credit hold at the policy's trigger — new orders for the account block per module 1's machinery (the limit and hold settings), the customer informed per the standard notice. A hold is a documented decision by the named role, and its purpose is stated plainly: stopping the exposure growing while the balance resolves.

4. Gear four — the resolution decision. Trigger: the ladder exhausts or the account disputes. Action: the owner's decision from the file — the negotiated settlement (a payment plan with dates, recorded and followed like promises), the dispute resolution through the document references, or the escalation to formal recovery per the policy. Write-offs, where reached, are the accountant's controlled entries with the owner's approval, and the account's credit posture resets per the ladder.

5. The collections reads. Weekly: the gear worklist — accounts by gear with next actions and promise dates due. Monthly: gear outcomes — amounts collected by gear, promises kept and broken, holds imposed and lifted; the figures file with the receivables summary. The procedure's measure is simple: overdue value falling, and no account reaching gear three whose gear-one contact was never made.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Worked example: invoicing the BizRetail Ltd order
lessons.html:
This chapter runs the module through the enterprise order modules 3-5 built: BizRetail Ltd, the 12-branch rollout, the 50/40/10 schedule, wave one delivered to five branches. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the advance invoice (Chapters 3, 5). Per the schedule and the site's configuration, the 50% advance portion was claimed at order and funded before the work queue took the order (module 4). The Payment Entry recorded the advance against the order; the advance sits identified on BizRetail Ltd's ledger awaiting allocation.

Step 2 — the delivery-portion invoice (Chapter 3). Wave one submitted (module 5): five branches, fifteen units, acknowledged. The invoicing run draws the wave from the delivered-not-billed list and bills the 40% delivery portion for the delivered branches from the wave's Delivery Notes — quantities per the notes, rates per the order (the 4% terminal concession intact through to the invoice rows), references carrying order and delivery per row. Taxes compute at the trade posture: net, VAT at 7.5%, gross — the arithmetic BizRetail Ltd's procurement office reconciles line by line.

Step 3 — the allocation (Chapter 5). The invoice prepares with its advance allocation: the advance applies against the delivery-portion claim per the schedule's arithmetic, and the invoice's balance due computes at the customer's terms. BizRetail Ltd's statement now reads in order: the order reference, the advance received, the wave invoice, the allocation, the balance at its due date.

Step 4 — the return's money side (Chapter 6). The damaged printer (module 5's return) was resolved by replacement, not credit — the return and replacement documents cross-reference, and no credit note issues because no value changed hands. The example states the rule by contrast: had the resolution been a return for credit, the credit note would have issued against the wave invoice for one printer at its invoiced rate, referenced to the return Delivery Note.

Step 5 — the gears in use (Chapters 7-8). The wave invoice crosses the value threshold, so gear one runs at 7 days before due: the pre-due contact confirms the invoice is in BizRetail Ltd's payment cycle with no queries — recorded. Payment arrives by transfer at terms; the Payment Entry records same-day and allocates per the remittance advice; the aging shows the account current. %billed advances on the order; waves two and three will repeat the cycle, and the 10% retention bills at completion per the milestone read.

The file. The order file now carries the full chain: quotation versions, the order and its amendment, five Delivery Notes and acknowledgments, the return pair, the advance entry, the wave invoice with its allocation, and the collections contacts — the account answerable end to end from one file, per the standing standard.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in invoicing and collections, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the typed due date. Symptom: due dates entered by hand; the aging computing from improvised dates; terms decisions bypassed. Correction: templates re-applied; the aging re-read. Prevention: due dates only from the terms template, per module 1.

Error 2 — billing beside the documents. Symptom: direct invoices for what should be order-and-delivery flows; quantities disagreeing with despatches; claims with no references. Correction: the chain reconstructed; the invoice corrected through the credit lane. Prevention: the three-path rule and the monthly direct-invoice sample.

Error 3 — the unallocated ledger. Symptom: payments and credits sitting unallocated beside open invoices; statements the customer disputes; the aging overstating exposure. Correction: the weekly unallocated read worked to zero against remittances. Prevention: allocation as part of recording, and advances allocated at each milestone invoice.

Error 4 — the silent short-pay. Symptom: customer deductions absorbed by under-allocation; disputes and rebates invisible in the record. Correction: the differences surfaced and routed — credit note or dispute lane. Prevention: partial allocations recorded as partial, with the difference's lane decided at recording.

Error 5 — the credit note without a return. Symptom: goods-related credits issued with no return document; stock and money records disagreeing about what came back. Correction: the return documented or the credit reversed. Prevention: the two-document rule and the return read listing credits against returns.

Error 6 — collections by memory. Symptom: contacts unrecorded; promises unfollowed; accounts reaching deep overdue with no gear history. Correction: the file reconstructed; the gears applied from the current state. Prevention: every contact recorded, the weekly gear worklist, and the gear-one discipline on qualifying invoices.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the invoice walk with honest dates, template due dates, and per-row references; choose the correct creation path and run the worklists to zero; state the four postings and the three correction lanes under the e-invoicing rules; record and allocate payments including advances and short-pays; operate the credit lane with the return tie and the credit-or-refund decision; read the aging and run the statement cycle; and run the four gears with their triggers and records.

Module rule 7: the invoice claims what the documents support — billed from the delivery or the schedule, due by the template, transmitted as the permanent record, settled by allocated payments and referenced credits, and collected by the four-gear procedure with every contact recorded. Module 8 covers bundles, blanket orders, and the advanced selling instruments.
